item.title: Toward Neutrino and Dark Matter Detection with Ancient Minerals: TEM Study of Heavy-Ion Tracks in Olivine
item.description: arXiv:2604.09732v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Solar, supernova, and atmospheric neutrinos, and possibly weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter, have been interacting in the Earth beneath our feet for billions of years. The ''paleo-detector'' technique seeks to detect and characterize the induced crystalline defects from these events, in particular from energetic nuclear recoils, which in some minerals can be preserved on these timescales. Such defects can manifest as nuclear recoil tracks, on the order of a few nanometers wide and extending up to hundreds of microns in length, which can be detected with nanoscale-resolution microscopy. In order to test the feasibility of the paleo-detector technique and to study the formation and morphology of track defects in promising mineral candidates like olivine, we use ion irradiation to artificially implant tracks to effectively mimic astrophysical particle interactions. We present a study of heavy-ion track width as a function of depth, which we relate to ion energy, in an olivine crystal irradiated with 15 MeV Au$^{+5}$ using scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Unlike previous studies, which measure tracks at the surface of the irradiated sample, we instead take measurements at various target depths via focused ion-beam sectioning of the irradiated sample. No etching techniques are used to enhance the tracks. In addition, we provide a comparison to predictions from simulations using SRIM software and previous results with a variety of ion species and energies. Notably, we find that a significant change in track continuity across the energy range studied (0.4-12.9 MeV) is indicative of the transition between electronic and nuclear stopping power dominance, consistent with the simulations' predictions. Overall, the tracks produced in olivine indicate that this mineral is an attractive candidate for paleo-detection, with robust track creation at the MeV scale.

item.title: Tails, Trails, and Transients: Comets, NEOs, and Supernovae in Rubin Early Data Preview 2
item.description: arXiv:2609.30361v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We identify effective single-visit imaging hidden within the deep coadded images of the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2). We develop a workflow to locate known small Solar System bodies in these data, using our Ponder orchestrator with the Sorcha survey simulator to predict their positions and the Rubin Science Platform to identify shallow coadds and extract image cutouts. Because cometary activity and near-Earth object (NEO) trails produce extended morphologies, both remain identifiable in shallow coadds. From approximately 700 comet cutouts, we identify 59 activity detections spanning 32 objects. We discover activity in 2025 NC6, previously unknown to be active, and independently rediscover two comets through their activity. We recover 336 NEO cutouts, including 29 with predicted trails over 25 pixels. We demonstrate how the same provenance-driven methods can recover stationary transients in Rubin coadds, including ones predating the alert stream. Of 47 publicly-reported transients coinciding with EDP2, 36 occupy shallow coadds. We show Rubin photometry agrees with published lightcurves to within 0.2 mag. The imaging provides additional bands, host-galaxy context, and deeper supernova pre-discovery limits than discovery surveys could reach. We showcase seven transients, including SN 2025nbh, which we identify as lying in the outskirts of AGC 114905, an ultra-diffuse galaxy central to the dark-matter-free debate; the supernova offers an independent galaxy distance measurement. Shallow coadds are a relatively unexplored facet of Rubin data with applications beyond the examples presented here; regions with varying numbers of contributing visits will persist throughout the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).

item.title: Deglobalising the fit: how to search for physics beyond vacuum General Relativity in LISA catalogues
item.description: arXiv:2610.27069v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna will observe up to $\sim 10^{7}$ overlapping signals, which have to be characterised simultaneously with a \emph{global} fit. This is a challenge for model comparison since rerunning the global fit for every model of interest, including deviations from vacuum General Relativity, is computationally demanding. An alternative is a two-step post-processing strategy: a first global fit with vacuum models only, after which selected target sources are reanalysed under a different model with all other sources subtracted. We show that in this strategy a beyond-vacuum effect in a target source can be partly absorbed by the overlapping \textit{nuisance} sources in the first fit, subtracted with them, and never reach the reanalysis. In the linear-signal approximation, the loss in reported detection significance is captured by a single number, the \emph{masking ratio} $\mathcal{R}\in[0,1]$: a deviation the global fit would detect at $n_\sigma$ is reported by post-processing at $\mathcal{R}\,n_\sigma$, and, for a single beyond-vacuum parameter, bounds in null tests are reported too tight by the same factor. We show how to compute $\mathcal{R}$ from the posterior samples of the vacuum global fit, and give an algorithm that ranks the nuisance sources by how much of the effect each can absorb, so that only the most correlated ones need to be refitted with the target. We validate our method with full Markov-chain Monte Carlo inference on a toy model of 21 overlapping chirping sinusoids, one of which carries a small non-linear chirp that represents the missed physics. Using our post-processing recipe, we are able to recover the global-fit result on the beyond-vacuum parameter to within $0.15\sigma$ by refitting only 4 of the 20 nuisance sources. This method can serve as a basis for tests of General Relativity in realistic LISA mock datasets.

item.title: Near-Quantum-Limited Readout for the Princeton Axion Search using a sub-GHz Kinetic Inductance Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier
item.description: arXiv:2611.06761v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parametric amplifiers are a workhorse for near-quantum-limited measurements above 1 GHz. However, amplifier development has been more limited below 1 GHz. We present a kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KI-TWPA) operating over 300-700 MHz, with gain exceeding 30 dB and pump powers of a few hundred nanowatts. The system noise performance, as measured by a variable-temperature noise source, is 2.5-3.5 quanta. This device is a versatile new tool for precision measurements of sub-GHz signals, with applications including readout of semiconductor spin qubits, superconducting detector arrays, and searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. We characterize aspects of the amplifier performance relevant to axion searches, including gain drift, compression point, amplifier noise at various operating temperatures, readout with an input circulator, and magnetic field insensitivity.

item.title: Different Stories: European Astronomy as a Tool of Colonization in the Americas and Hawai'i
item.description: arXiv:2611.21687v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The history of Western astronomy is frequently told as a story of discovery, technological innovation, and human progress. Yet the astronomical knowledge, instruments, and techniques associated with these achievements also contributed to European colonial expansion. Through four material and visual examples - a marine chronometer, an astronomical surveying quadrant, the Nautical Almanac, and contemporary observatories on Maunakea - we invite reconsideration of astronomy's relationships with navigation, territorial mapping, colonial authority, and Indigenous lands. How might these histories be told differently when considered through Indigenous Knowledges and Perspectives? What might such reconsideration reveal about the continuing relationships between astronomy, colonialism, and place?
item.dc:creator: Gregg A. Wade, D. Lussier

item.title: Diffusing the assumptions: towards realistic LISA stochastic component separation with physics-aware simulation-based inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.27848v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simultaneous global-fit inference of the numerous sources observed by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) depends on accurate modeling of its stochastic components: instrumental noise, the Galactic foreground, and astrophysical or stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds (SGWB). Realistic features such as non-Gaussian transients and data gaps challenge traditional likelihood-based pipelines, creating an opportunity for simulation-based inference (SBI) to augment traditional analyses. Here, we present an SBI framework for LISA stochastic component separation built on the Simformer, a transformer trained with diffusion or flow matching that ingests the full time-delay interferometry cross-spectral matrix via a physics-aware embedding. We progressively relax standard simplifying assumptions on simulated 11.6-day datasets containing a loud foreground and a faint power-law SGWB. With unequal arms and per-link noise freedom, the networks match 17-dimensional MCMC posteriors after importance reweighting; full cross-spectra constrain each link's optical metrology noise amplitude to $1\%$. When marginalizing over glitches or massive black hole binary transients, estimation errors remain flat up to transient signal-to-noise ratios of several hundred, whereas ignoring them severely biases likelihood fits. Under time-varying spline noise levels, realistic glitch rates, and gaps up to one day long, posterior coverage remains nominal or conservative across $\sim 10^4$ simulations. We test coverage in the local neighborhood of a given observation by introducing a novel importance-weighted localized simulation-based calibration test. We find flow matching slightly better calibrated than diffusion in simpler regimes and observe modest gains from physics-aware template inputs. Finally, we outline how these networks can initialize the noise and stochastic blocks of a LISA global fit.
